description: EN/A1 independently drafted Asteroids Reading test; not reviewed by second teacher.

tabs.title: Understanding the message
tabs.description: Interpret the passage and its purpose.

tabs.title: Reasons and connections
tabs.description: Find explanations supported by the text.

tabs.title: Use what you have read
tabs.description: Apply the information to new situations.

questions.q: Why is an asteroid different from a star?
choices: It travels very close to Earth.
It does not make its own light.
It is always bigger than a mountain.
It stays in the same place.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that asteroids are rocks and do not produce light as stars do.

questions.q: What can we learn about the size of asteroids?
choices: All asteroids are as small as cars.
The largest asteroids are smaller than cars.
Every asteroid is bigger than Earth.
Some are small and others are very large.
questions.explanation: The passage compares some asteroids with cars and others with mountains.

questions.q: What do scientists learn by watching an asteroid move?
choices: The colour of its light.
The age of the Sun.
The path it follows in space.
The number of people on Earth.
questions.explanation: Observing changing positions helps scientists learn an asteroid's orbit.

questions.q: Which fact makes Ceres different from most asteroids?
choices: Ceres is round, while many other asteroids have irregular shapes.
Ceres is the only space rock that goes around the Sun.
Ceres is so small that scientists cannot see it.
Ceres enters the air above Earth every year.
questions.explanation: Ceres is round and classed as a dwarf planet, while most asteroids are not round.

questions.q: Why do scientists use large telescopes?
choices: To make space rocks move faster.
To see objects that are very far away.
To make the night sky darker.
To find mountains on Earth.
questions.explanation: A telescope makes distant objects easier to see.

questions.q: Why is a meteorite interesting to a museum visitor?
choices: It can make its own light at night.
It is always larger than a car.
It is a very old piece of space rock that reached Earth.
It is a living thing from another planet.
questions.explanation: The text describes a museum meteorite as a dark, heavy and extremely old piece of space rock.

questions.q: Why do many small space rocks not reach the ground?
choices: They stop moving near Earth.
Telescopes catch them in the sky.
They return to the asteroid belt.
They burn in the air around Earth.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says many small pieces burn up before reaching the ground.

questions.q: You hear that a large asteroid will hit Earth tomorrow. What should you remember from the passage?
choices: All news about asteroids is false.
Very big impacts are rare, and scientists watch the sky.
Asteroids cannot come near Earth.
Every asteroid is visible without a telescope.
questions.explanation: The text says major hits are rare and scientists monitor the sky to learn more and help keep people safe.

questions.q: You see a small light moving slowly in a series of telescope photos. What might scientists study?
choices: Whether it follows an orbit around the Sun.
Whether it will turn into a star tomorrow.
Whether the Moon has made the light.
Whether it is larger than every mountain.
questions.explanation: Scientists compare pictures to find the paths followed by objects in space.

questions.q: Why is looking at a clear night sky a good idea at the end of the story?
choices: It helps us stop all asteroids.
It makes a big asteroid hit less likely.
It lets us see Ceres with our eyes.
It can make us curious and ask questions about space.
questions.explanation: The writer encourages readers to look at the sky and ask questions about space.
